# Dash illumination LED swap and color change

> **[Unverified]** This page rests on a single community report. Cross-check before relying on it.

> Items marked **[Partial]** are only partly confirmed by the source and need more work. They stay in the review queue and are firmed up, corrected or removed as more sources come in.

## Summary

[Partial] Swap dash illumination LEDs and change color by sanding gauge faces to remove blue tinting. [t2218]

## Procedure

> **[Partial]** Needs more work: the verifier could confirm only part of this procedure (the steps marked [Partial], or whether the list is complete). Steps or precautions may be wrong or missing; read the source thread before relying on it. Later runs fill it in as more sources are found.

1. [Partial] Remove the speedometer cluster by snapping it apart.
2. Use a fork to gently pry the needles straight up from their seats.
3. Sand the back of the gauge faces with 220 grit sandpaper to remove blue tinting caused by incandescent light reflection.
4. Install new LEDs into the lighting circuit, ensuring wires are soldered directly for power.

_Procedure reported by [t2218]._

## Tools

- [Partial] Fork [t2218]
- 220 grit sandpaper [t2218]

## Parts

- #74 size LED bulbs, wedge base: 3 diodes, 160° beam pattern [t2218]
- 194 bulb, optional upgrade for full 360° dispersion [t2218]
- LED strips, for climate controls [t2218]

## Specifications

- **Bulb base size (stock)**: #74 [t2218] ([Unverified] single report)
- **Sandpaper grit**: 220 [t2218] ([Unverified] single report)

## Tips & gotchas

- [Partial] Sand only until the blue tint is gone; be gentle so cutouts on the front remain unaffected. [t2218]
- [Partial] Use a fork to gently pry needles straight up without breaking them. [t2218]
- Note that green LEDs work best on tinted materials because they contain blue and yellow components. [t2218]

## Common mistakes

- Using LEDs with colors far from the gauge material's pigment (e.g., blue LED for orange needles) without sanding first, resulting in poorly lit gauges. [t2218]
- [Partial] Ignoring that incandescent bulbs emit 360° light while standard #74 LEDs have a limited viewing radius of about 160°, causing hot-spotting. [t2218]
- [Partial] Using white or blue LEDs on unsanded gauge faces, which causes uneven lighting due to the back's blue tint blocking specific colors. [t2218]
- [Partial] Encountering a dead spot in light distribution with #74 bulbs if not seated correctly against the dispersion material. [t2218]
